How did people tell time before mechanical clocks?
a: Before mechanical clocks, people told time using natural phenomena and simple instruments. The most ancient method was the sundial, which tracked time by the position of the sun's shadow cast by a vertical stick or gnomon. Sundials were used by ancient Egyptians as early as 1500 BCE and were accurate during daylight hours, but they didn't work at night or on cloudy days. To address this limitation, the ancient Egyptians and Babylonians developed water clocks, or clepsydrae, which measured time by the flow of water from one container to another. These were the first devices that could measure time at night and indoors. Water clocks ranged from simple bowls with small holes to sophisticated systems with floating indicators and gear mechanisms. The ancient Greeks and Romans improved water clocks with mechanical gears and dials, creating the first analog timekeeping devices. Candle clocks were another method, used in China and elsewhere — marked candles would burn for a known duration, and the position of the wax indicated the passage of time. Hourglasses, which used sand flowing between two glass bulbs, were widely used in medieval Europe and on ships for measuring short intervals. The Chinese invented incense clocks, which used incense sticks that burned at a known rate and could also indicate time through scents and bells. Monks in medieval monasteries used canonical hours marked by bells to structure their daily routines. In ancient China, large water-powered clock towers with automata and celestial displays were built as early as the 8th century CE. The development of these timekeeping methods was driven by the needs of agriculture, navigation, religious observance, and commerce. The transition to mechanical clocks in the 13th century marked a revolution in precision, but the fundamental principle — measuring time through natural or mechanical processes — remained the same.
